angular-momentum-s2.title: Torque on a wheel over time
angular-momentum-s2.text: A wheel (I = 0.50 kg·m²) starts at rest on a frictionless axle. The graph shows the net torque on it, counterclockwise positive.

items.q: What is the size of the puck’s angular momentum about point P? Give the value and its unit.

mistakes.why: Value: that is the linear momentum, mv. Multiply by the lever arm: L = mvd.
Value: d is not squared for a point object. L = r m v sin θ = mvd.

why.correct: L = rmv sin θ = mv(r sin θ) = mvd = (0.20 kg)(3.0 m/s)(0.40 m) = 0.24 kg·m²/s.

items.q: As the puck slides on past P, its distance r from P grows. Its angular momentum about P
options: stays the same, because r sin θ stays 0.40 m
grows, because r grows
shrinks, because the puck moves away from P
is zero, because the puck is not turning

why.correct: L = rmv sin θ, and r sin θ is the perpendicular distance from P to the line of motion, 0.40 m at every position. With m and v constant, L about P stays 0.24 kg·m²/s.
options: Right: the perpendicular distance from P to the path never changes.
r grows, but sin θ shrinks so that r sin θ stays 0.40 m.
Moving away along a straight line keeps the lever arm, and so L, the same.
A point object moving past a point has angular momentum about it, turning or not.

items.q: What is the puck’s angular momentum about point Q, which lies on its path?
options: Zero
0.24 kg·m²/s
0.60 kg·m²/s
It depends on how far the puck is from Q

why.correct: The puck’s velocity points along the line through Q, so the perpendicular distance from Q to its line of motion is zero: L = mv(0) = 0. Angular momentum depends on the point you choose.
options: Right: the puck moves straight along a line through Q, so θ = 0 or 180°.
That is the value about P. About Q the lever arm is zero.
That is the linear momentum, mv, in kg·m/s.
Along a line through Q, r sin θ = 0 at every distance.

items.q: A second puck of the same mass slides at 6.0 m/s along a parallel line 0.20 m from P. Compared with the first puck, its angular momentum about P is
options: the same
twice as large
half as large
four times as large
Right: twice the speed × half the lever arm.
The speed doubles, but the lever arm halves.
The lever arm halves, but the speed doubles.
L = mvd is the product; the two factors cancel.

items.q: What angular impulse does the torque deliver from 0 to 2.0 s?

mistakes.why: Value: that divides torque by time. Angular impulse is τΔt, the area under the τ-t graph.

why.correct: Angular impulse = τΔt = (4.0 N·m)(2.0 s) = 8.0 N·m·s = 8.0 kg·m²/s, the area under the graph.

items.q: The wheel starts at rest. What is its angular velocity at 3.0 s?

mistakes.why: Value: that multiplies L by I. ω = L/I.
Value: that uses the torque for 3.0 s. The torque is zero after 2.0 s.

why.correct: From 0 to 2.0 s, ΔL = 8.0 kg·m²/s; from 2.0 to 3.0 s the torque is zero, so L stays 8.0. ω = L/I = (8.0 kg·m²/s)/(0.50 kg·m²) = 16 rad/s.

items.q: What is the wheel’s angular momentum at 6.0 s?

mistakes.why: Value: that adds the last part of the area. From 4.0 to 6.0 s the torque is negative, so it removes angular momentum.
Value: that ignores the negative torque from 4.0 to 6.0 s.

why.correct: Add the signed areas: +8.0 (0-2 s) + 0 (2-4 s) + (−2.0 N·m)(2.0 s) = 4.0 kg·m²/s.

items.q: Which describes the graph of the wheel’s angular momentum against time from 4.0 s to 6.0 s?
options: A straight line sloping down, with slope −2.0 N·m
A horizontal line, because L is conserved
A straight line sloping up, because the wheel still turns counterclockwise
A vertical drop to zero at 4.0 s

why.correct: τ_net = ΔL/Δt is the slope of the L-t graph. A constant −2.0 N·m makes L fall in a straight line from 8.0 to 4.0 kg·m²/s; the wheel slows but still turns the same way.
options: Right: the slope of L-t is the net torque.
The net torque is not zero in this interval, so L changes.
L is still positive but falling; the slope is the torque, −2.0 N·m.
A finite torque changes L gradually, at a rate equal to the torque.

items.q: For a rigid object turning about a fixed axis, angular momentum is
options: L = Iω, in kg·m²/s
L = ½Iω², in joules
L = Iα, in N·m
L = mv, in kg·m/s

why.correct: L = Iω pairs I with m and ω with v, as p = mv does. Its unit is kg·m²/s (the same as N·m·s and J·s).
options: Right: the rotational partner of p = mv.
That is rotational kinetic energy.
Iα is the net torque.
That is linear momentum.

items.q: A bicycle wheel with I = 0.25 kg·m² spins at 12 rad/s. What is its angular momentum?

mistakes.why: Value: that is ½Iω², the kinetic energy in joules. L = Iω.

items.q: A torque of 0.60 N·m acts on a spinning top for 0.50 s in the direction it spins. By how much does its angular momentum change?

mistakes.why: Value: that divides torque by time. ΔL = τΔt.

items.q: A ball on a string moves in a horizontal circle of radius 0.50 m at 2.0 m/s around a post. A student says the ball has no angular momentum about the post because it is a point object, not a spinning body. Which response is correct?
options: It does: about the post, L = rmv sin 90° = rmv
It does not: a point object has no rotational inertia
It does not: its velocity keeps changing direction
It does, but just while the string is speeding it up

why.correct: A point object has angular momentum about a chosen point: L = rmv sin θ. Moving around the post, its velocity is perpendicular to r, so L = rmv. (Treating it as I = mr² turning at ω = v/r gives the same result.)
options: Right: a point object has angular momentum about any point it does not move straight toward or away from.
L = Iω is for rigid bodies; a point object has L = rmv sin θ.
Changing direction does not remove angular momentum; here its size stays the same.
It has angular momentum whenever it moves past the post, speeding up or not.

items.q: A graph of a wheel’s angular momentum against time is a horizontal line. What does that tell you?
options: The net torque on the wheel is zero
The wheel is not turning
The wheel’s angular acceleration is constant and nonzero
A constant torque is acting on the wheel

why.correct: τ_net = ΔL/Δt, the slope of the L-t graph. A horizontal line has zero slope, so the net torque is zero and ω is constant.
options: Right: the slope of L-t is the net torque.
A horizontal line at a nonzero L means steady turning.
Constant nonzero α would make L change steadily, a sloped line.
A constant nonzero torque gives a sloped straight line.

items.q: Two wheels have the same angular momentum. Wheel A has twice the rotational inertia of wheel B. Wheel A’s angular velocity is
options: half of wheel B’s
twice wheel B’s
the same as wheel B’s
one quarter of wheel B’s

why.correct: ω = L/I. With L the same and I doubled, ω is halved.
options: Right: ω = L/I.
A larger I with the same L means a smaller ω.
Same L, different I, different ω.
ω is inversely proportional to I, not I².

items.q: A torque acts on a wheel for a short time. Which change in the wheel is set directly by the angular impulse τΔt?
options: Its change in angular momentum
Its change in rotational kinetic energy
Its rotational inertia
Its angular acceleration

why.correct: The angular impulse-momentum theorem: τΔt = ΔL. (The work τΔθ is what changes the kinetic energy.)
options: Right: angular impulse = ΔL.
Kinetic energy changes by the work, τΔθ, not by τΔt.
I depends on the mass distribution, not on the torque.
α = τ/I is set by the torque itself, not by τΔt.

items.q: A puck slides in a straight line at constant speed past a point P on a frictionless table. Predict how each quantity changes as the puck moves from far left of P to the point of its path closest to P.

variables.name: The puck’s distance r from P
variables.why: The puck approaches the closest point of its path to P, so r shrinks to the perpendicular distance d.

variables.name: sin θ, where θ is the angle between the puck’s velocity and the line from P to the puck
variables.why: Far away, that line is nearly parallel to the path (θ near 180°, sin θ near 0); at the closest point θ = 90° and sin θ = 1.

variables.name: The puck’s angular momentum about P
variables.why: L = rmv sin θ, and r sin θ always equals the fixed distance d from P to the path, so L = mvd does not change.

why.correct: With no net force, mv is constant. As the puck approaches, r falls while sin θ rises, and their product r sin θ stays equal to the fixed distance d, so L = mvd about P stays the same.
